chunks: He was asked about what the dove had drunk from. So he said: 'Everything whose flesh may be eaten — perform wudu from its residue and drink from it.'

And (he was asked) about what a falcon, or a hawk, or an eagle had drunk from. So he said: 'Everything from the birds — perform wudu from what it drinks, except if you see blood in its beak. So if you see blood in its beak, do not perform wudu from it and do not drink.'

key_terms.الْحَمَامَة: Al-hamama — dove or pigeon; a bird whose flesh is permissible (halal) to eat, hence its su'r is considered pure
key_terms.بَاز/صَقْر/عُقَاب: Baz (falcon), Saqr (hawk), Uqab (eagle) — birds of prey; their flesh is generally forbidden, yet their su'r is ruled pure unless blood is seen in the beak
key_terms.سُؤْر: Su'r — the residue or leftover water from which an animal has drunk; its ritual purity status is a topic of classical fiqh
key_terms.مِنْقَار: Minqar — beak; visible blood here is the condition (illa) that renders the water impure

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to perform wudu from water that a bird of prey has drunk from in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) gives a legal ruling on ritual purity concerning the residue water (su'r) of birds. The general principle is that any bird whose flesh is permissible to eat — such as doves — leaves behind pure water suitable for wudu and drinking. However, for birds of prey like falcons, hawks, and eagles, the water remains pure unless there is visible blood on the bird's beak, which would indicate ritual impurity. This ruling reflects the classical Shia jurisprudential method of deriving purity rulings from the permissibility of eating an animal's flesh.

en.hubeali: Ahmad Bin Idrees and Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Muhammad Bin Ahmad, from Ahmad Bin Al Hassan, from Amro Bin Saeed, from Musaddaq Bin Sadaqa, from Ammar Bin Musa, (It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullahasws having been asked about what the doves had drunk from. So heasws said: ‘Everything the flesh of which can be eaten, so you can perform Ablution (Wudhu) from its residue, and drink from.

And about what has been drunk from by the falcon, or an hawk, or an eagle, so heasws said: ‘Everything from the bird which they have drunk from, you can perform Ablution (Wudhu) from it, except if you were to see blood in its beak. So if you were to see blood in its beak, then you can neither perform Ablution (Wudhu) from it nor can you drink’.
en.sarwar: 5. Ahmad ibn Idris and Muhammad ibn Yahya have narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hassan from ‘Arm ibn Sa‘id from Musaddiq ibn Sadaqah from ‘Ammar ibn Musa who has said the following: “Once abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, was asked about the leftover of the water from which pigeons have drunk. He (the Imam) said, ‘It is permissible for you to use the leftover from which edible animals have used. You can use it for Wudu’ or drink the leftover of the water from which they have drunk, like a falcon or a hawk or an eagle.’
He (the Imam) then said, ‘You can use for Wudu’ the water from which birds have drunk, unless you see blood on their beaks. If so then do not use it for Wudu’ or drinking.’”
